bodyText:
What is an Algorithm

An algorithm is a finite, well-defined sequence of steps that takes an input, performs computation, and produces an output. Every algorithm must terminate, be unambiguous, and be effective, meaning each step can actually be carried out. Algorithm design paradigms are general strategies for constructing algorithms. The three most commonly asked paradigms in PPSC examinations are the greedy method, divide and conquer, and dynamic programming (DP). Each paradigm suits a different kind of problem, and examiners frequently test whether a candidate can identify which paradigm fits a given problem.

The Greedy Method

A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step, always making the locally optimal choice at each step in the hope that these local choices lead to a globally optimal solution. A greedy algorithm is correct only when the problem has two properties: the greedy-choice property, meaning a locally optimal choice can be part of a globally optimal solution, and optimal substructure, meaning an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to its subproblems. Classic greedy algorithms include Kruskal's algorithm for the minimum spanning tree, published by Joseph Kruskal in 1956, Prim's algorithm, published by Robert Prim in 1957, Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm, developed by Edsger Dijkstra in 1956 and published in 1959, and Huffman coding, developed by David Huffman in 1952 for data compression. Other standard greedy examples are activity selection, fractional knapsack, and job sequencing with deadlines. Note that the 0/1 knapsack problem cannot be solved correctly by a greedy method; it requires dynamic programming.

Divide and Conquer

Divide and conquer solves a problem in three steps: divide the problem into smaller subproblems of the same type, conquer the subproblems recursively, and combine their solutions into a solution for the original problem. Merge sort, developed by John von Neumann in 1945, is the classic example: it divides the array in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges the sorted halves in linear time, giving a time complexity of O(n log n) in all cases. Quicksort, developed by Tony Hoare in 1959, partitions the array around a pivot and sorts the partitions recursively; its average-case complexity is O(n log n) but its worst case is O(n squared). Binary search is also a divide-and-conquer algorithm, reducing the search space by half at each step for a complexity of O(log n) on a sorted array. The efficiency of divide-and-conquer algorithms is usually analysed with recurrence relations, often solved using the Master Theorem.

Dynamic Programming (DP)

Dynamic programming, a term introduced by Richard Bellman in the 1950s, solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem only once, and storing its result for reuse. It applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. The two implementation styles are memoization, a top-down approach that stores results of recursive calls, and tabulation, a bottom-up approach that fills a table iteratively. Classic DP problems include the Fibonacci sequence, the 0/1 knapsack problem, longest common subsequence, matrix chain multiplication, and the Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest-path algorithm. DP differs from divide and conquer in that divide and conquer solves independent subproblems, while DP reuses solutions to overlapping subproblems, which is why DP is far more efficient for problems such as Fibonacci, where naive recursion takes exponential time but DP takes linear time.

Choosing the Right Paradigm

For examination questions, use the following guide: if the problem asks for a locally optimal choice that never needs revision, such as activity selection or minimum spanning tree, think greedy. If the problem splits cleanly into independent smaller problems, such as sorting or searching, think divide and conquer. If the same subproblem recurs many times and an optimal solution is built from optimal subsolutions, such as knapsack or longest common subsequence, think dynamic programming. A common trap is to apply a greedy method to the 0/1 knapsack or to coin change with arbitrary denominations, where greedy fails; greedy works for coin change only with canonical coin systems such as standard currency denominations.

bodyText:
Why Complexity Analysis Matters

Complexity analysis measures how the running time or memory use of an algorithm grows as the input size, usually denoted by n, grows. It allows algorithms to be compared independently of hardware, programming language, or implementation details. Time complexity counts the number of basic operations as a function of n, while space complexity counts the extra memory used. Examiners focus on worst-case analysis most often, because it gives a guarantee, but best-case and average-case analyses are also asked.

Asymptotic Notations: Big-O, Big-Omega and Big-Theta

Big-O notation describes an upper bound on growth: f(n) is O(g(n)) if f(n) grows no faster than g(n) up to a constant factor for large n. Big-Omega describes a lower bound: f(n) is Omega(g(n)) if f(n) grows at least as fast as g(n). Big-Theta describes a tight bound: f(n) is Theta(g(n)) if it is both O(g(n)) and Omega(g(n)). Big-O notation was introduced by Paul Bachmann in 1894 and popularised by Edmund Landau, which is why it is sometimes called Landau notation. Little-o and little-omega are stricter, non-tight versions of Big-O and Big-Omega. In practice, candidates should state Big-O for an upper bound and Big-Theta when the bound is tight, for example merge sort is Theta(n log n).

Common Complexity Classes

Complexities are ordered from fastest to slowest growth as follows: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n) linearithmic, O(n squared) quadratic, O(n cubed) cubic, O(2 to the power n) exponential, and O(n factorial) factorial. O(1) means the time does not depend on input size, as in accessing an array element by index. O(log n) arises when the problem size is halved at each step, as in binary search. O(n log n) is the best possible comparison-based sorting complexity and is achieved by merge sort and heapsort. Exponential and factorial complexities are infeasible for large inputs and characterise brute-force solutions to hard problems.

Best, Average and Worst Cases

Best-case complexity is the minimum time over all inputs of size n, average-case is the expected time over all inputs, and worst-case is the maximum time. For example, linear search has best case O(1) when the target is first, average case O(n), and worst case O(n) when the target is last or absent. Quicksort has best and average case O(n log n) but worst case O(n squared) when the pivot is repeatedly the smallest or largest element. Bubble sort, selection sort and insertion sort all have worst-case O(n squared) time, while insertion sort has best case O(n) on an already sorted array. Space complexity is also tested: merge sort needs O(n) auxiliary space, while quicksort needs O(log n) stack space on average.

bodyText:
Graphs and Traversal Basics

A graph consists of vertices, also called nodes, and edges connecting them. It may be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and connected or disconnected. Graph traversal means visiting every vertex exactly once in a systematic order. The two fundamental traversal algorithms are breadth-first search (BFS) and depth-first search (DFS). Both run in O(V + E) time for a graph with V vertices and E edges when implemented with an adjacency list. Traversal is the foundation for many applications, including shortest paths, connectivity testing, cycle detection, and topological sorting.

Breadth-First Search (BFS)

BFS explores a graph level by level, visiting all neighbours of a vertex before moving to the next level. It uses a queue, a first-in first-out structure, and marks vertices as visited to avoid revisiting them. BFS finds the shortest path, in terms of number of edges, from the source to every other vertex in an unweighted graph. It also tests whether a graph is connected, finds connected components, and can test whether a graph is bipartite. BFS is the basis of shortest-path finding in unweighted networks and of the level-order traversal of trees.

Depth-First Search (DFS)

DFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack, either explicitly or through recursion, which follows a last-in first-out order. DFS is used for topological sorting of directed acyclic graphs, detecting cycles, finding strongly connected components, solving mazes, and testing connectivity. In an undirected graph, DFS classifies edges as tree edges and back edges; the presence of a back edge indicates a cycle. DFS also underlies many recursive algorithms, including the detection of articulation points and bridges in a network.

Dijkstra's Shortest-Path Algorithm

Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a single source to all other vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It was developed by Edsger Dijkstra in 1956 and published in 1959. It maintains a set of vertices whose shortest distance is finalised and repeatedly selects the unvisited vertex with the smallest tentative distance, relaxing its outgoing edges. With a binary heap priority queue, its time complexity is O((V + E) log V); with a Fibonacci heap it is O(E + V log V). Dijkstra's algorithm fails on graphs with negative edge weights; for those, the Bellman-Ford algorithm, which runs in O(V times E) time and can detect negative cycles, must be used instead.

Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithm

A spanning tree of a connected graph connects all vertices with exactly V minus 1 edges and no cycles, and a minimum spanning tree (MST) is the spanning tree of minimum total weight. Kruskal's algorithm, published by Joseph Kruskal in 1956, is a greedy algorithm: it sorts all edges by weight in ascending order and adds each edge to the MST if it does not form a cycle, using a disjoint-set union, also called union-find, data structure to test for cycles efficiently. Its complexity is dominated by sorting, giving O(E log E) time. Kruskal's algorithm is commonly contrasted with Prim's algorithm, published in 1957, which grows a single tree from a starting vertex. Both produce an MST, but Kruskal processes edges globally while Prim grows one tree vertex by vertex.

bodyText:
What is Hashing

Hashing is a technique that maps a key to an index in a table, called a hash table, using a hash function. The index is called the hash value or hash code, and it determines where the key and its associated value are stored. A good hash function distributes keys uniformly across the table, is fast to compute, and is deterministic, meaning the same key always maps to the same index. Hashing is the foundation of dictionaries, symbol tables, database indexing, caches, and sets in most programming languages.

Hash Functions and Load Factor

Common hash function methods include the division method, which uses the remainder of the key divided by the table size, the multiplication method, and folding, which splits the key into parts and adds them. The load factor of a hash table is the number of stored elements divided by the table size, denoted by alpha equals n divided by m. As the load factor rises, collisions become more likely and performance degrades, so tables are typically resized, or rehashed, when the load factor passes a threshold. Choosing a prime number as the table size helps the division method distribute keys more evenly.

Collision Resolution

A collision occurs when two different keys map to the same index. Separate chaining resolves collisions by storing all keys that hash to the same index in a linked list, or another structure, at that slot. Open addressing stores all keys directly in the table itself and probes for another empty slot on collision. The three standard open-addressing probe sequences are linear probing, which checks the next consecutive slots, quadratic probing, which checks slots at increasing squared offsets, and double hashing, which uses a second hash function to determine the step size. Linear probing suffers from primary clustering, where consecutive occupied slots form long runs, while quadratic probing suffers from secondary clustering. Double hashing generally distributes probes best among the three.

Performance and Applications

With a good hash function and a controlled load factor, the average-case time for search, insertion, and deletion in a hash table is O(1), constant time, which is why hashing is preferred over balanced trees for simple lookup. The worst case, however, is O(n), when all keys collide into a single slot, as in a poorly designed hash function under adversarial input. Hash tables are used for symbol tables in compilers, database indexes, caching, password storage with salted hashes, spell checkers, and counting frequencies. A frequent examination distinction is between hashing, which gives average O(1) lookup but no ordering, and balanced search trees, which give O(log n) lookup but keep keys sorted.

bodyText:
Complexity Classes P and NP

Class P is the set of decision problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic algorithm, meaning the running time is bounded by a polynomial in the input size, such as O(n squared) or O(n cubed). Class NP is the set of decision problems whose proposed solutions can be verified in polynomial time, equivalently, problems solvable in polynomial time by a non-deterministic algorithm. Every problem in P is also in NP, because a problem that can be solved quickly can certainly have its solution verified quickly, so P is a subset of NP. Whether P equals NP is one of the most famous open questions in computer science and mathematics, and it is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems announced by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, carrying a prize of one million US dollars.

Polynomial-Time Reductions and NP-Completeness

A problem A reduces in polynomial time to a problem B if any instance of A can be transformed into an instance of B in polynomial time, so that solving B also solves A. A problem is NP-hard if every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time, meaning it is at least as hard as every problem in NP. A problem is NP-complete if it is both in NP and NP-hard: its solutions can be verified in polynomial time, and every NP problem reduces to it. The first problem proved NP-complete was the Boolean satisfiability problem, SAT, by Stephen Cook in 1971 in the Cook-Levin theorem, with Leonid Levin independently proving a similar result. In 1972, Richard Karp showed 21 further problems to be NP-complete, including the travelling salesperson decision problem, the Hamiltonian cycle problem, graph colouring, and the clique problem.

NP-Hard vs NP-Complete

The key distinction for examinations is that NP-complete problems are in NP, while NP-hard problems need not be. The optimisation version of the travelling salesperson problem, finding the shortest possible tour, is NP-hard but not NP-complete, because NP-completeness is defined only for decision problems, those with a yes or no answer. The decision version, asking whether a tour shorter than a given length exists, is NP-complete. Similarly, the halting problem is NP-hard but is not in NP at all, because it is undecidable. If any NP-complete problem were found to have a polynomial-time algorithm, then every problem in NP would also be solvable in polynomial time, proving P equals NP. Conversely, if P does not equal NP, as most researchers believe, then no NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm.

Why This Matters for Problem Solving

Recognising a problem as NP-complete changes the strategy: instead of searching for an exact polynomial-time algorithm, which is believed not to exist, practitioners use approximation algorithms, heuristics, backtracking with pruning, or exponential algorithms that are acceptable for small inputs. Classic NP-complete problems asked in examinations include SAT, 3-SAT, the travelling salesperson decision problem, Hamiltonian cycle, vertex cover, subset sum, knapsack decision, graph colouring, and clique. The knapsack decision problem, asking whether a subset of items fits a capacity with a value above a threshold, is NP-complete, while the optimisation version is NP-hard. Candidates should be able to define P, NP, NP-hard and NP-complete, name the Cook-Levin theorem, and explain why proving a problem NP-complete shows it is unlikely to have an efficient exact solution.
